# 2 Samuel Chapter 12 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 180v–181v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_012_page_001.jpg, 2SA_012_page_002.jpg, 2SA_012_page_003.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** The LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor.

**2** The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

**3** but the poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up with him and with his children. It ate of his morsel, drank from his cup, and lay in his bosom, and it was like a daughter to him.

**4** Now a traveler came to the rich man, but he was unwilling to take from his own flock or his own herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."

**5** David's anger burned greatly against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die! **6** He shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and because he had no pity."

**7** Nathan said to David, "You are the man! Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul. **8** I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms, and I gave you the house of Israel and Judah. And if that had been too little, I would have added to you as much again.

**9** Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his eyes? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife. You have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.

**10** Now therefore, the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'

**11** "Thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. **12** For you did it in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"

**13** David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die. **14** Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall surely die."

**15** Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became ill.

**16** David pleaded with God on behalf of the child. David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground. **17** The elders of his household stood over him to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them.

**18** On the seventh day the child died. The servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "While the child was still alive, we spoke to him and he would not listen to us. How then can we tell him the child is dead? He may do himself harm."

**19** But David saw that his servants were whispering together, and David perceived that the child was dead. David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead."

**20** Then David arose from the ground and washed and anointed himself and changed his garments. He went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. Then he went to his own house, and when he asked, they set food before him and he ate.

**21** His servants said to him, "What is this that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive, but when the child died, you arose and ate food."

**22** He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me, and the child may live.'

**23** But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."

**24** Then David comforted Bathsheba his wife and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him.

**25** He sent word by the hand of Nathan the prophet, who called his name Jedidiah — "beloved of the LORD" — for the LORD's sake.

**26** Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city. **27** Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah and have captured the city of waters. **28** Now gather the rest of the people and encamp against the city and capture it, lest I capture the city and it be called by my name."

**29** So David gathered all the people and went to Rabbah and fought against it and captured it. **30** He took the crown of their king from his head — its weight was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone — and it was set on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.

**31** He brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron threshing sledges and iron axes, and made them work at the brick-kilns. Thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators agree on the chapter's tripartite structure: Nathan's parable and confrontation (vv.1-14), the death of the child and David's response (vv.15-23), and the birth of Solomon with the Rabbah epilogue (vv.24-31). The key theological moments — *attah ha-ish* (v.7), *chatati la-YHWH* (v.13), *va-YHWH ahevo* (v.24) — are consistently recognized. The *tiqqun soferim* in v.14 is noted by all three translators. The transition from judgment (the death of the first child) to grace (the LORD's love for Solomon) is the theological pivot of the chapter and is handled with appropriate weight by all.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.3 — "morsel" vs. "plate"
- **EMET:** "From-his-morsel she-ate"
- **LOGOS:** "It ate of his morsel"
- **PNEUMA:** "She ate from his plate"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "It ate of his morsel" — *mippitto* means "from his morsel/piece." LOGOS preserves the Hebrew image. PNEUMA's "plate" modernizes away from the intimacy of shared food.

### V.4 — "traveler" vs. "wayfarer" vs. "visitor"
- **EMET:** "a-traveler [helekh]... the-wayfarer [oreach]"
- **LOGOS:** "a traveler... the wayfarer"
- **PNEUMA:** "a traveler... his visitor"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "a traveler... the guest" — *helekh* = traveler (v.4a); *oreach* = wayfarer/guest (v.4b). The two Hebrew words are distinct. "Guest" captures *oreach* while being more natural than "wayfarer."

### V.5 — "son of death" vs. "deserves to die"
- **EMET:** "a-son of-death [ben-mavet]"
- **LOGOS:** "deserves to die"
- **PNEUMA:** "deserves to die"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "deserves to die" — *ben-mavet* is an idiom meaning "worthy of death." The literal "son of death" is opaque in English. LOGOS/PNEUMA capture the meaning correctly.

### V.8 — "into your bosom" vs. "into your arms"
- **EMET:** "into-your-bosom"
- **LOGOS:** "into your arms"
- **PNEUMA:** "in your arms"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "into your arms" — *be-cheqekha* can mean "into your bosom/lap/arms." "Arms" (LOGOS) is more natural while preserving the intimacy of the image.

### V.9 — "despised" vs. "treated with contempt"
- **EMET:** "have-you-despised [bazita]"
- **LOGOS:** "have you despised"
- **PNEUMA:** "did you treat... with contempt"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "have you despised" — *bazah* = to despise/treat with contempt. EMET/LOGOS's "despised" is more forceful and fits prophetic speech.

### V.13 — "put away" vs. "taken away"
- **EMET:** "has-passed-over [he'evir] your-sin"
- **LOGOS:** "has put away your sin"
- **PNEUMA:** "has taken away your sin"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "has put away your sin" — *he'evir* (hiphil of *avar*) means "caused to pass over/removed." LOGOS's "put away" preserves the formal gravity of the divine act. PNEUMA's "taken away" is acceptable but less precise.

### V.14 — *tiqqun soferim* — "enemies of the LORD" vs. "the LORD"
- **EMET:** preserves MT "the-enemies of-YHWH" with textual note
- **LOGOS:** "the LORD" (translates probable original)
- **PNEUMA:** "the LORD" (translates probable original)
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the LORD" — the phrase "enemies of the LORD" is a widely recognized *tiqqun soferim*. The original reading, attested by the scribal tradition itself, was that David scorned YHWH directly. LOGOS/PNEUMA correctly restore the sense.

### V.16 — "sought God" vs. "pleaded with God" vs. "begged God"
- **EMET:** "sought David God [Elohim]"
- **LOGOS:** "David pleaded with God"
- **PNEUMA:** "David begged God"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "David pleaded with God" — *vayevaqesh David et-ha-Elohim* means "David sought God." In context, "pleaded" (LOGOS) captures the urgency without PNEUMA's desperation.

### V.18 — "he will do evil" vs. "do himself harm" vs. "do something desperate"
- **EMET:** "And-he-will-do evil [vera'ah]"
- **LOGOS:** "He may do himself harm"
- **PNEUMA:** "He might do something desperate"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "He may do himself harm" — the Hebrew *ve-asah ra'ah* (he will do evil/harm) is ambiguous. LOGOS reads it as self-harm, which fits the servants' fear. PNEUMA's "desperate" is also reasonable. EMET's literal rendering is unclear.

### V.24 — "called his name Solomon" vs. "named him Solomon"
- **EMET:** "called his-name Shelomoh"
- **LOGOS:** "he called his name Solomon"
- **PNEUMA:** "David named him Solomon"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "he called his name Solomon" — preserves the Hebrew construction *vayiqra et-shemo*. PNEUMA's specification of "David" as subject is interpretive (the Hebrew pronoun is ambiguous — it could be David or Bathsheba).

### V.25 — Jedidiah meaning
- **EMET:** "Yedidyah [beloved of-YHWH]"
- **LOGOS:** "Jedidiah"
- **PNEUMA:** "Jedidiah — 'Beloved of the LORD'"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Jedidiah — 'beloved of the LORD'" — following PNEUMA in providing the meaning in-line, as the name's theology is essential to the narrative.

### V.30 — "their king" vs. "Milcom"
- **EMET:** "their-king [malkam]" (notes Milcom variant)
- **LOGOS:** "their king"
- **PNEUMA:** "their king"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "their king" — *malkam* is vocalized as "their king" in the MT. The Ammonite deity reading (Milcom) is possible but not supported by the Leningrad Codex pointing.

### V.31 — forced labor vs. execution
- **EMET:** preserves MT ambiguity with "set them at the saw"
- **LOGOS:** "set them to labor with saws"
- **PNEUMA:** "put them to work with saws"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "set them to labor with saws" — the MT *vayasem* (he set/placed) supports forced labor rather than execution. This reading is consistent with the brick-kiln reference and ancient Near Eastern practice.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
